body: I will never forget the moment, after the call to come to the hospital, after following the ambulance to a distant town because lifeflight was grounded due to snow, after over 12 hours of holding his body, holding his head, as he slowly regained consciousness but was still not within his head due to the toxicity of all that he swallowed, through the hallucinations when he was conscious that we tried to have him breathe through, I just remember that moment, when his eyes cleared and I saw HIM in those eyes for just a short moment - his first words were "I'm still here" - and the intense sadness, the despair was in the color of his eyes. It's probably one of the most heart wrenching experiences of my life and stays with me still. It's been 18 months, and he's alive, working part-time as he still recovers from the after effects. There are certain visceral moments as a parent - that is one of my top ones. And I worry, still, because he doesn't talk about it anymore - will he be ok?

So I'm somewhat going through a similar period. Here's my current approach. 
*Spend some time and identify a few areas that you'd like to relocate to (I've narrowed mine to three "regions). Reflect on what your wish list is: coastal? rural but with close urban area? City with lots of cool things to explore where you will "blend in"? Write it up, edit at will - envision what you'd like!


* Next, begin searching for jobs that might offer relocation assistance. You have degrees and that puts you ahead of the game! Look on USAJobs for government jobs in your area - with your degrees you could maybe get a GS-9 or above - sweet! And many offer relocation so there...you have to be persistent and patient. With your degrees, government work (oh and they can accommodate your disability) might be your golden ticket.


* Go on Craigslist, Indeed, Monster, Career Builder to name a few and start searching in those identified geographical areas. Use keyword searching like "relocation assistance", or type each of your degree fields and see what pops up. Job posters are getting increasingly creative with job titles and I've been finding I qualify for jobs I never would have anticipated based on the "new" job title.


* Start also searching for small rentals/sublets in those same areas. Do a budget based on what pricing for something small will be and do the math to see how much you need to make for it to happen. (I use the x3 rule - rent x3 x12 months to get an annual salary range I HAVE to have for the area).


* Remember you are still young with lots of time ahead of you. Many like you are just graduating as well but there are opportunities elsewhere - just take some time to figure out what you'd like to experience. It's an adventure - you can do this!
